title: The bland Tao
hookLine: music and fine food stop travelers, but the Tao is bland and never runs out (Tao Te Ching 35)

lines: ONIONS AND A BAND AT A STREET FAIR.
cards: Onions frying at a street fair. A band warming up by the food trucks. People who were walking somewhere else slow down, drift over, and stand there for a while with paper plates.
An hour later they're gone, off to the next thing, and the band is packing up. Then, at home that night, somebody drinks a plain glass of water at the kitchen sink. Nobody photographs it.
Nobody drifts over to watch. Chapter thirty-five of the Tao Te Ching sets those two scenes side by side, and it makes a surprising claim about which one lasts.

teach.h: THE WORLD COMES, AND FINDS EASE.
teach.b: First, the great image. The chapter says that whoever holds the great image of the Tao, the whole world comes to them. And those who come find no harm there, only rest, peace and ease.
Not excitement. Ease. Second, the street fair.

teach.h: MUSIC AND TREATS STOP THE PASSING GUEST.
teach.b: In James Legge's translation: "Music and dainties will make the passing guest stop (for a time)." Dainties is an old word for treats. Notice the chapter doesn't condemn them.
Music is good. Treats are good. They really do stop people.
But the guest is passing, and the stop is for a time. Third, the bland part.

teach.h: THE TAO SEEMS FLAT AND FLAVORLESS.
teach.b: The chapter says the Tao, when it's put into words, seems flat and has no flavor. Look at it, and it doesn't seem worth looking at. Listen, and it doesn't seem worth hearing.
That's an odd thing for a book about the Tao to say about the Tao. It doesn't try to sell it. Fourth, the turn.
After all that, the chapter's last words, in Legge's version: "the use of it is inexhaustible." The music ends. The plate gets empty.
The plain thing never runs out. Back at the street fair, the chapter isn't against any of it: loud, salty, bright, gone by evening.

teach.h: THE USE OF IT IS INEXHAUSTIBLE.
teach.b: It just sets the plain thing beside it. The chapter names no examples, but some readers think of the plain things nobody would post. Water.
Sleep. A walk. The same friend, again.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-five as an invitation to value plain, ordinary things, which seem dull beside entertainment and treats but do not run out.

o: a rule to eat only plain food and water
flavorless in words, yet its use never ends
a dull teaching meant only for beginners

p: stop the passing guest for a time

s: chapter thirty-five says music and fine food are bad
it only says they make the passing guest stop for a time.
the chapter says the Tao seems flavorless but never runs out
the chapter says those who come to the great image find excitement
it says they find no harm, only rest, peace and ease.

games.q: you're a traveler on the road. there's music at an inn and food on the fire. what does chapter thirty-five say happens?
o: you stop there for a while.
games.why: music and dainties make the passing guest stop, for a time. the guest moves on; the plain Tao is the thing that doesn't run out.

practice: If there's water nearby, take a sip and hold it a moment before you swallow; if not, notice the plain feeling of air coming in through your nose. Don't look for anything special.
Stay with something that has almost no flavor, and see how much is there anyway: coolness, weight, the breath after.

wordCard.voice: The bland Tao. Chapter thirty-five's claim that the Tao, put into words, seems flavorless and not worth a look, and yet its use never runs out. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: plain, thin, weak in flavor; chapter thirty-five's word for how the Tao tastes.

carryVoice: Your line: bland and endless. Plain doesn't mean small, and it doesn't run out. Until tomorrow.
